new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Mauwake has an empty rule and no existing statements, so this supplies a placement (second syllable, predictable, non-phonemic) where the catalog has none. It is a secondary report of Berghäll 2015: 42, which is the primary source; Berghäll's actual rule is 'the syllable containing the second vowel', i.e. an initial long vowel or diphthong takes the stress, which Pick's 'second syllable' wording drops.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress in Mauwake is predictable and falls on the second syllable of words of two or more syllables (Pick's one-line summary of Berghäll 2015: 42). Pick adds nothing of his own on Mauwake stress; on p. 134 he mentions that consonant clusters arise from elision of an unstressed vowel (citing Berghäll 2015: 41).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Mauwake. Pick states (p. 32) that he has 'little else to say about stress in Northern Adelbert languages' and that data on stress in most languages of the group are minimal; the exceptions he discusses concern Pamosu (Tupper 2012) and phonemic stress in Usan (Reesink 1987), not Mauwake.
new_statements.identity_note: Berghäll 2015 describes Mauwake (also called Ulingan) of the Madang Province north coast, c. 2,000+ speakers; she notes only minor dialectal variation (e.g. /y/ realized [ʒ~j]) and does not restrict the stress statement to a dialect. Pick 2020 treats Mauwake as a member of his 'Kumil' / Northern Adelbert group and relies on Berghäll's data; his own fieldwork was on other Northern Adelbert languages (Barem, Manep, Waskia, Gavak etc.), not Mauwake.

new_statements.quote: Stress is not phonemic in Mauwake, but three degrees of phonetic stress are discernible in a word. Primary stress is marked by greater intensity, higher fundamental frequency and often, but not always, by non-phonemic lengthening of the vowel. [p. 34] ... In words of two or more syllables, the syllable containing the second vowel is stressed. Thus the first syllable is stressed if it contains a geminate vowel (46a) or a diphthong (46b). In all the other cases the second syllable is stressed (46c). When the stressed syllable is long, the stress falls equally on the whole vowel sequence (46d–e). [p. 42] Examples (46): /aasa/ [ˈaː.sa] 'canoe'; /kuija/ [ˈkui.ja] 'it bites'; /aɸura/ [a.ˈɸu.ra] 'lime'; /siowa/ [si.ˈo.wa] 'dog'.

new_statements.relation_note: Fills the catalog's empty rule for Mauwake with the primary statement: non-phonemic stress on the syllable containing the second vowel (second mora), i.e. second syllable unless the initial syllable is long (VV or diphthong), plus secondary stress in compounds and reduplications. Compatible with Pick's 'second syllable' summary but more precise: it is mora-counting, so the placement is weight-sensitive rather than strictly fixed: second syllable.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-phonemic. In words of two or more syllables the syllable containing the second vowel (second mora) carries primary stress: if the first syllable has a geminate (long) vowel or a diphthong it is stressed, otherwise the second syllable is stressed; in a long stressed syllable the stress spreads over the whole vowel sequence. Affixes take primary stress when they sit in that position; clitics never do (a monosyllabic short-vowel host keeps the stress when a clitic attaches). Mauwake is not tonal. Clausal/sentence stress is a separate pragmatic prominence, by default on the verb or non-verbal predicate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes (p. 42): 'Compound words and some reduplicated words also have a secondary stress. In the second (and third) compound of a compound word, that syllable has a secondary stress which in a single word would receive primary stress (49).' Also, when a long initial syllable is reduplicated as a whole, the second syllable is long and takes secondary stress (50), e.g. /kui-kuisow/ [ˈkui.ˈˈkui.sow] 'a few'. Three degrees of phonetic stress are distinguished (primary, secondary, unstressed).
new_statements.exceptions: Clitics never receive stress (p. 42). In §2.1 the placement rule is called 'otherwise exceptionless'. Word-final unstressed /a/ is elided before a vowel-initial word (p. 43); 'In some cases even a stressed /a/ is elided, and the stress moves to the following vowel in the utterance. This mainly happens with the accusative pronouns, which tend towards cliticization' (pp. 43-44). Unstressed vowels may be elided, yielding surface consonant clusters (p. 41).
new_statements.identity_note: Berghäll 2015 describes Mauwake (also called Ulingan) of the Madang Province north coast, c. 2,000+ speakers; she notes only minor dialectal variation (e.g. /y/ realized [ʒ~j]) and does not restrict the stress statement to a dialect. Pick 2020 treats Mauwake as a member of his 'Kumil' / Northern Adelbert group and relies on Berghäll's data; his own fieldwork was on other Northern Adelbert languages (Barem, Manep, Waskia, Gavak etc.), not Mauwake.

readall_conflicts: No real disagreement. Pick (2020: 31) summarizes Berghäll (2015: 42) as 'stress.. falling on the second syllable (in words of two syllables or longer)', which is a simplification: Berghäll's rule is that the syllable containing the SECOND VOWEL is stressed, so words with an initial geminate vowel or diphthong (/aasa/ [ˈaː.sa], /kuija/ [ˈkui.ja]) take initial stress. Read literally, Pick's wording would predict *[aˈa.sa]; Berghäll's is the primary statement and should govern. Both agree that stress is predictable and non-phonemic and that Mauwake is not tonal. Järvinen 1989 (the same author's unpublished phonology manuscript, tagged 'likely states stress') could not be opened (not reachable by automated download at every SIL URL tried), so its wording is unverified; Berghäll 2015 is by the same author and almost certainly supersedes it.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the stated page (book p. 42 / PDF p. 58, sec. 2.3.1; domain quote p. 34 / PDF p. 50). The deciding source is a modern 516-page open-access reference grammar by the long-term fieldworker, the top item in Glottolog's descriptive bibliography; every other descriptive reference is by the same two SIL authors and either unpublished (1980, 1989 mss) or the 2010 thesis that the 2015 book supersedes. The classification (classification weight, left edge, CVV heavy: stress on the syllable containing the second vowel, i.e. initial if geminate vowel/diphthong else second syllable; affixes count, clitics do not; secondary stress in compounds/reduplication) matches the source text exactly, and the grammar calls the rule 'otherwise exceptionless'. No better source exists to change it; only a low-priority wish for the author's 1989 unpublished phonology ms.
